It is not only farm products that go to these countries. In Toronto they are building a complete new mill to be set up in India. In Montreal a complete textile mill is being built. I understand that a further 2,000 or
3.000	men would have been employed in Montreal in one plant if they had been able to sell an order for heavy material in the Far East. While they lost that order it indicates that can be done. I know there are other people besides the farmers in this country. My heart aches for the man who cannot get a job. I fear and shudder to think of the return of the days when men will be standing at factory gates waiting for jobs, good men, intelligent men, honest men.
If there is anything we can do, we should do it. I think the Minister of Finance will admit that it would not do any harm. Surely he is not so careful about the treasury of Canada especially when we have groups flying
26.000	or 27,000 miles. The cost of this would not be so great. If you think it would not do any harm, we suggest that it might do some good. If it will do some good, if it will help the farmers of Canada, if it will help the factories of this country to sell articles in the sterling areas, if it will give work to men, then I believe it is the thing to do.
Great Britain has consistently given us great favourable trade balances for three-quarters of a century and I urge the government not to lightly pass that off. If I have the privilege of being in this house much longer

I hope I shall never hear again what we heard in the thirties, that we must not provoke the United States. They do not like us any better when we take that attitude. They expect us to mind our own business. They expect us to be strong. They expect us to be grown up. Canada is the greatest producing nation in the world for its population. We are a proud people and we never have provoked the United States of America. We live on a friendly basis beside them and we have great trade relationships with them.
But they have cut our products off overnight. That was not done in any spirit of antagonism or bitterness; it was done because they had to save their own markets. Only two weeks ago it was stated in congress that when a commodity became surplus it would not be allowed into the country. I would like to know what was written in the Geneva agreement which is in effect now before it has even been ratified by parliament. I would like to know what is in that agreement that says, when the man from Texas or Oklahoma states he has more beef or bacon than he knows what to do with: "Keep your steers down in Texas because we are going to buy from the Canadians. They have been very nice to us and have never provoked us so you can keep your cattle on the ranch because we are going to buy from the boys in Canada". Stop and think about it, Mr. Speaker. It has happened now two or three times, and it is in no spirit of antagonism that I suggest it may happen again. It is just because the United States minds its own economic business. They want and expect us to be economically strong, and they believe we are capable of minding our business.

Mr. Speaker, the question before the house this afternoon is one of great importance to Canada. I certainly think it is too important to be brushed aside in the manner in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has just treated the entire question. In a recent poll of public opinion it was shown that there is no other public question today with which our people are so much concerned as that of the loss of our markets. That is not surprising because over the years governments and political parties have been dinning into the ears of our people the importance of our export markets. The reason why our people place so much importance on the loss of them today is that they are associated in their minds with employment. There is a fear in Canada today that their loss will simply be the forerunner of unemployment and another depression such as we experienced in the thirties.

The minister has rejected the amendment. He has suggested that, although there may be no harm, certainly no good could come out of the calling of another conference as recommended by the amendment. He informed us that the government is already in possession of all the information that could possibly be obtained in such a meeting. In other words, he has told us that such a conference would be a mere waste of time. Then he suggested that possibly the Conservatives would be formulating the policy of that conference, and he asked the mover of the amendment to tell him what the agenda for it would be. He suggested he would not want to attend another conference to deal with subjects such as were dealt with in the thirties. Surely there is a difference. I am rather surprised that the minister should even suggest that the Conservatives would have any voice in determining the agenda. Can you imagine the great Liberal government of today asking the handful of Conservatives on this side of the house to suggest the agenda for a conference initiated by the government? Surely the government would be in a position, if it called such a meeting, to determine exactly what subjects should be put before it for discussion.
Of course the minister also forgets that since 1930 the Conservative party has become the Progressive Conservative party, and it is not beyond the realm of possibility that even concerning the matter of foreign conferences the Conservatives may have become much more progressive than they were in the dark days of the depression. Unless the minister can suggest some other alternative for meeting the problem, then I am prepared to support the amendment even at the risk of the Conservatives dictating to the Liberals what the nature of the conference should be.
Our problem today is one of finding markets for our goods. The minister has told us clearly that there are only certain ways in which we can hope to sell our goods to other countries. We must take their goods in return. If, as is the case in many countries which need our surplus goods today, they just have not the goods to give us in return, then we must find other means whereby they can pay us for our products in some way. The export of our surplus products is so essential to the economy of Canada that I submit the house should not allow the motion to go into supply to pass until the government show us that they have something to put before the house that, in their opinion, is a solution to the problem, if the amendment is not the answer to it.
The minister says that we can export our goods by lending dollars to these countries,
Trade
but he told us that our supply of dollars is not sufficient to warrant our doing so. He told us we could borrow from the United States and lend the money to the countries wanting to purchase our goods, but he suggests that is not the solution and that no one wants to do so. He suggested that a third possibility was the reduction of consumption within our own country in order to accumulate money that we could lend. He suggested that the reduction of consumption in Canada would put us in a better position to lend to those countries that want to buy our goods, but he did not suggest that the government would even entertain the idea of advancing that as a solution to the problem.
I want to say to the minister that in my opinion the Canadian public are far out in front of the government in this respect. It is no credit to us as a nation, and I am quite sure the Canadian people do not consider it creditable, that we should attempt to consume all of our own production that we possibly can while millions of people in other parts of the world are in want, and when at the same time we have surpluses of goods that we ourselves cannot consume and which we cannot sell to them. It might not be as impossible, as the minister suggests, to institute a modified program of austerity in this country whereby we can provide these other countries that need our surpluses with the means to purchase them. I suggested that if the government are not prepared to accept the amendment they should come forward with some other concrete policy to show us that they are taking measures to meet the problem facing the country today.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that the matter now up for discussion is of such importance to the future of Canada and the well-being of the Canadian people that I should say just a few things in connection with it. I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) should be congratulated on bringing this most important question of Canada's trade before the house today. Before I conclude I shall have a brief word to say on the amendment the hon. member moved; but, Mr. Speaker, I have been tremendously surprised at the jaunty attitude this government has displayed towards this most important question facing Canada today, the question of our trade.
My colleague from Acadia (Mr. Quelch) mentioned that step by step this situation has been developing over a period of years. It is nothing new that has suddenly come to our attention. Our trade predicament today has grown up over so many years that if people in administrative positions had been watching the situation and had been free and willing

Trade
to take independent action, facing the facts, the present situation could have been alleviated and our predicament could have been avoided. Back in 1946 the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, had this to say in his report dated February 8 of that year:
Looking to the future, however, there is no reason for complacency. Most of our real problems of post-war adjustment are still ahead. The backlog of demand will not be large in relation to productive capacity when industry has been fully reconverted and inventories built up to normal levels. When the time lag involved in demobilization is over, government expenditures will fall rapidly. Nor will our foreign lending to finance the purchase of Canadian goods remain indefinitely at the present level. The prevailing optimism on the North American continent is dangerous if it diverts attention from the problems which have to be faced.
That is the end of the warning which was given by the governor of the Bank of Canada away back in 1946. That warning has become a prophecy; and the last part of Mr. Towers' statement has been vindicated in the action and lack of action by the government opposite. The Liberal government has continued to consistently disregard the warnings not only of Mr. Towers but of others who saw the situation developing. We do not have to start in 1946; we can go back further than that and point out to this government definite actions they took which have had the cumulative effect of precipitating the present bad trade situation.
With respect to the proposal of the hon. member for Lake Centre, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) says he does not want to go to a conference unless he knows exactly what the conference is going to do. The minister was not a member of the government back in 1944, but he was on the government side of the house. At that time, when the conference was called at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, did the government say they would not take part in that conference without knowing exactly what it was going to do? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that they jumped into that conference; they not only went down completely ignorant of what it was going to do but came back completely befuddled and confused as to what it had done. If anyone wants proof of that statement all that is necessary is to go back to 1945 and read the debates that took place in this house in connection with the Bretton Woods proposal.
So I say that while the present minister was not there, he must assume some responsibility for what was done; and let me say just one other thing about this business of not knowing what a conference is going to do. Following the war Canadian influence throughout
CMr. Low.]
the world was great. There has never been a time when Canada's word, Canada's counsel or Canada's warning has meant so much. At that time the people of the world would have been likely to heed what Canada said. Well, if at that time Canada had used her influence to see to it that a clause something like this was written into the Bretton Woods agreement: "The creditor nations agree that it is their obligation to accept goods and services in payment for the goods and services they export, and that this obligation will be continuously recognized and observed", I feel satisfied that something of the kind would have been included. But instead of using our influence in that way we plunged in without full recognition of what that agreement was going to do to us and how impossible it would be for the convertibility of currencies to take care of the trade situation which was developing, since the United States insisted upon following the program she had been following for quite a number of years, a program which they think must have attached to it a favourable balance of trade for the U.S.A. every year.
Well, sir, everyone knows that if the United States is not going to buy enough goods in the markets of the world to provide the other nations with dollars, then those other nations cannot buy from the United States, or from Canada. That was patently clear at the time, so I am going to ask the minister why the Canadian delegation went to Bretton Woods without knowing a single thing about what the proposals would be, and why it came away without any definite idea of what it had done. I do not see why in the world he should be afraid of a conference such as that suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I would not want to go to a conference without knowing something of what was proposed, of course; but getting a definite idea of what the agenda might be would not be out of the question. I believe if the government showed some inclination to sit down and discuss this whole thing honestly and straightforwardly with all parties in this house, an acceptable agenda could be drafted; and I am satisfied that such an agenda could be made also acceptable to the other members of the commonwealth.
The minister says the Geneva agreements have been of the greatest benefit to Canada; and as an example he cited the increase in our trade with the United States which has resulted from certain tariff concessions. That is perhaps one of the good results; but I will say the minister certainly has a fetish on Geneva, and I do not think he can possibly

justify the weakness in the non-discrimination clause. The great weakness in the nondiscrimination feature of the Geneva agreements is that it does not permit a country like Canada to choose her source of supply. Nor does it permit any other country that is a party to it to choose its source of supply. I do not believe it is right in a world which is now crying for fair dealing in trade. As a matter of fact, I thought that the Minister of Finance would be the last person in Canada to try to defend the non-discrimination features of the Geneva agreements, because he was caught in the meshes of it in 1947. Not only that, but he put Canada in a most ridiculous position, by making it impossible for Canadians to buy their own production without paying a tax on it, simply to placate certain interests in the United States who insisted on the Geneva non-discrimination clause.
The Minister of Finance should be the last man to defend that clause, because it prohibited Canadians from buying green vegetables and tomatoes in the fall of 1947, since the minister had prohibited their entry from the United States, in order to protect our dwindling supply of United States dollars. The Canadian people have not forgotten that. They are the people who are demanding that the minister justify that with something more than the assertion that we benefited greatly by having tariff reductions. Those tariff reductions could have been made without the nondiscrimination clause. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that any country in this world that wants to be fair and' just in its trade relationship will not insist upon a non-discrimination clause. Such a country will first see what sort of reductions can be made in. the tariffs without the necessity of such a clause. There would be no need for the non-discrimination clause, if the United States and other creditor nations were to fully recognize their responsibilities in a world in which trade is so seriously unbalanced as ours. This unbalance arises mainly from the serious unbalance in industrial capacity.
I do feel that the United States is not bound to follow the policy which she has been following for many years, that is a policy of economic conquest. Surely it would be possible for Canada, with her influence, to stand up and say that we will enter into negotiations to make trade easier and to help remove the restrictions, provided you will not insist upon this diabolical non-discrimination clause. The minister mentioned Canadian cattle going to the United States. He suggested that the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was perhaps wrong in his assumption, because of the fact
Trade
that the United States was ready to take in many of the cattle from, his own constituency. Let me say that the United States ought to be the last to put an embargo against the entry of Canadian cattle into that country. It is a creditor nation and has a favourable balance of trade, which we do not have. I do not take what the minister said too seriously.

speechtext: Discrimination, can work both ways.

The sort of discrimination the minister suggests is the same sort as Pat said he was going to exercise against the railroad. He said he was going to buy a return ticket, and he was not going back. It is discrimination to balance trade, of course, not unbalance it. The Minister of Finance stated that if we were to accept sterling it is likely we would have to reduce consumption within Canada. I do not take the same .position as the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I should like to draw to the attention of this house the surpluses that are here in reality, or that could be here, but for the policies of this government-policies of taxation and restriction that discourage production.
I should1 like to read briefly from what the Minister of Agriculture said in a speech before the Canadian chamber of commerce in London in 1948.
It is difficult for us to understand, wily anyone should expect us to be other than disappointed with the 1949 contracts. They provide for 160 million pounds of bacon, for 50 million pounds of cheese, and no cattle or beef.
A little further along, he says:
There are no dollars available in the United Kingdom with which to purchase Canadian apples. Partly because of this we have financed the pulling out of 240,000 apple trees in Nova Scotia. There are no dollars available with which to purchase Canadian fish.
I suppose if it were possible to pull out the fish beds, the government would do that, and pay for it. It is a policy of discouraging and restricting production. I say that when you do that you are making it impossible for the Canadian people to help a world that is sadly lacking in food.
It is important for us to keep in mind that the minister went over to England, and negotiated with the British people, not for 160 million pounds of bacon. At another point in his speech the minister said:
All of our discussions on food bulk contracts were proceeding satisfactorily until difficulties arose in adjusting the relationship between dollars and sterling. We were aiming at being able to provide the United Kingdom with 350 million pounds of bacon, 125 million pounds of cheese, 75 million dozens of eggs and having 400,000 head, of cattle which we could dispose of either to the United States or the United Kingdom.

Instead of that, we had to sign a contract for 160 million pounds of bacon and 50 million pounds of cheese. There is no question about it, if the market had been provided under an agreement, the Canadian farmers would have put up the 350 million pounds of bacon. They would have produced to the utmost of their capabilities if the market had been there, and if taxation and other government policies had not been imposed upon them which restricted that production. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that these amounts of food, which have gone unproduced, could be looked upon as at least potential surpluses of goods that would have been available to send to these other countries, making it unnecessary to do what the minister said, reduce consumption. In the light of what has happened, I believe that is stupid in the extreme. I would say that no pound of food should go unproduced, so long as there is a need for it or a market for it anywhere in the world. No man should go unemployed for the lack of producing those things, as long as there is a willingness on the part of other people to buy and consume those things.
There is no question but what we could accept sterling, and finance it internally until such time as that blocked or non-convertible sterling could be traded around the sterling area for goods that we could bring back to this country. I have not been convinced by any argument to the contrary thus far. I would refer the Minister of Agriculture to one other thing. At the C.F.A. conference which took place in Niagara last month, it was brought to the attention of the delegates that poultry production had been reduced by 8 to 12 per cent, because of the failure to keep our markets with Britain. That is a serious reduction. It represents an amount of poultry and egg production that could well be available for trading if it had not been restricted by the fear that there would be no market. When I say, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot just look at the situation as it is, but must look at it as it could be under the proper inducements, you will see what I mean.
Before I close, there is one other thing I should like to mention. In common with the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) and others who have spoken, I believe that if the government feels this proposed conference is not the answer to our trading problem, if it does not hold out any hope for the success of such conference, the government should bring forward a program that will do something. Until that is done, my followers in this house and myself can do nothing else but support the motion put before us by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).

In supporting this amendment, Mr. Speaker, which has been moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), I must join with those who have preceded me in saying that they are unable to understand the reasoning and the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in his apparently ill considered and certainly very quick dismissal of the idea of holding at this time a commonwealth conference to discuss trade and related matters.
As I took note of the minister's remarks, he said in effect that he could not see that any good purpose would be served at the present time by having more conferences. It seems to me that the thing we should bear in mind is that, so far, we have not had since 1932 a trade conference of the type envisaged. We have not had a full-scale commonwealth trade conference since then. It is true that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), as he told us in his report recently on his trip to southeast Asia, did discuss or talk about trade matters with the other representatives there; but the fact is that that conference was not called to deal with trade matters. There were no trade experts there. Certainly the impression given was that, so far as trade was discussed, it was an informal discussion and trade was discussed as a side issue. It certainly was not the main subject of the conference. Indeed, from what the minister told us in his report, it became obvious that not only with regard to trade but even with regard to the matters that they did meet to discuss, they had neither intended nor apparently expected to reach agreement. Indeed, he told us that it was rather nice to sit down at the conference table and find out how far apart the different views were without actually coming to blows because of those differences; whether it was merely because the countries concerned were commonwealth countries or whether the tea had something to do with it, the minister did not tell us; but it seemed to me to be an approach to a conference that was almost certain to lead to negative results.
Before coming to the subject matter of the resolution itself, I should like to refer to one other point raised by the leader of the C.C.F. party in his remarks when he said, as I understood him, that he agreed in principle with the amendment but that he would not be able to support it unless it was clear that it was not necessarily a motion in support of the building up of a tariff structure. That matter has been dealt with by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) in his remarks following the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). But if further assurance is necessary, then as far as I can give

it-and I can speak for myself, at any rate- I can say that I would not support the motion or speak in support of it if I understood that such was its intent. But I do not understand that to be its intent. I understand it to be a motion advocating the summoning of a conference to discuss ways and means of eliminating trade barriers between the commonwealth countries, and as nothing more nor less than that. In that respect it is the very opposite of a high-tariff conference.
It seems to me that the motion calling for a conference is justified by the fact that the two thoughts uppermost in the minds of the Canadian people at the present time are, first, the increasing unemployment figures and, second, the loss of markets and the declining farm prices with which this country is faced. It was said recently, and I think it is certainly true, that it is not advisable nor desirable, particularly in the House of Commons, to emphasize fears, doubts and dismay as to the future. That is not my purpose in mentioning these two facts of unemployment and declining trade; but certainly those two problems do exist, and, in the minds of our people, they are large.
We shall not solve those problems unless we consider them, discuss them and meet them fairly and squarely. If we do that, Mr. Speaker, I for my part believe that we in Canada can solve our problems. I believe that those problems will disappear if we adopt the policies which can build this country into a great and prosperous trading nation, the senior partner in the commonwealth, the friend and ally of the United States. But as firmly as I believe that Canada can be made into that type of country, I believe that if we drift, if we allow this present tendency to continue, not only shall we not achieve that ambition, but we are in danger of facing conditions which are much worse than they are today.
In dealing with these two problems of unemployment and falling farm prices, may I say that it seems to me they are both the result of the same fact, namely, that we are losing our markets, particularly those in the commonwealth and sterling countries. In the same way they result from a remarkable unbalance in the Canadian economy, in the sense that we produce, particularly in the field of agriculture, far more than we can consume at home; and because of that fact we are dependent, as perhaps no other country is, to such a large extent upon overseas markets for what we produce. Our history up to the present has been one of constantly recurring surpluses in that those markets slip away for
Trade
one reason or another, and we are left with large quantities of surpluses here at home for which we can find no sale.
I want to discuss the situation both generally under the heading of this amendment before the house and particularly with reference to a problem which is vital to the area from which I come, namely, the problem facing our apple growers. There we have again, as we had in the 1930's and several times prior to that, a condition of recurring surpluses resulting entirely from the sudden loss of a market. As you know, Mr. Speaker, an apple grower's program is one taking from seven to twelve years to come to maturity. The marketing program of the orchardist cannot be changed overnight, because his tree takes some seven to eight years to come into bearing at all, and at least twelve years before it is bearing fully. He is therefore not in the happy position of some other producers who can change their program overnight. When his markets are lost, there is nothing he can do about it. That is the situation facing our apple growers in this country, particularly those in British Columbia today.
It is with that in mind that I want to discuss this resolution suggesting that we have a conference of commonwealth countries to discuss our trade problems, because our great market for apples has always been the United Kingdom. Unless we can restore that market, we are not going to solve the problem facing our particular growers.

Mr. *Speaker, I should like to say a word or two on

this bill. As I said last year, while there are eighteen members from British Columbia no one was prepared to sponsor a bill to permit the building of a pipe line unless it was built over an all-Canadian route. It would appear tonight that that was the unanimous feeling of those members. I am not familiar with the rules of the house, except those that I break. This is not a political bill, yet it was not possible to secure a British Columbia member to sponsor it.
It was only by the indulgence of some of us who believe in an all-Canadian route that the house waited for the hon. member to move the second reading. I am a rather junior member of the house, having been here only since 1940, but it is the first time in my experience that we have had to wait for a sponsor of a bill to make the motion for second reading.
They had to go across this great country of Canada to find a sponsor for this bill, and finally they settled on one from the middle province. I have a great deal of admiration for Manitoba because my father and mother were married there. That was the best thing that ever happened to Manitoba. Any province that can inspire two people to bring into the world the great member for Fraser Valley must have something within its boundaries.
Cold weather.

A few remarks are being made by some of my Manitoba associates. As I said before, while there are eighteen members from British Columbia, not one would sponsor this particular bill, bighearted as we are out there. We have often bled for the maritimes and we have contributed to central Canada. Tonight out of our bigheartedness we waited for the bill to be called. I was almost going to sponsor it myself because I felt it should not be lost in the wilderness.
My attitude to the bill is the same as it was last year. I have no hesitation in so stating and no apology to offer. At the last session some of us were accused of staging a filibuster on this measure. Personally I do not think we did, but nevertheless, together with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), may I say that I have no apology to offer for staging a filibuster if it is necessary in order to secure the best results for my riding and my province and if it is in the best economic interests of Canada. It is one of the few weapons a private member has when the interests of his riding and his province are involved.
Some remarks have been made, although belatedly, by the sponsor of the bill. I can appreciate that they hesitated to put before the house what they thought was right. If I

were the sponsor of a measure which was not in the best interests of western Canada, or of the majority of the people of the country as a whole, I too would hesitate before appearing to introduce the bill to the house. I want to make myself perfectly clear. I was criticized by some at the last session when I took the same stand that I am taking tonight. I am speaking tonight as the member for the constituency of Fraser Valley, and for no other riding in the province of British Columbia. Nevertheless I think I have the same right as any other member from that province to speak on its behalf. I want to make it clear I am speaking tonight in the interests of my own riding, and I say without fear of contradiction from anyone that I have the full support of each and every individual in the Fraser valley in the stand I am taking, irrespective of party, creed or race. I want to make that clear because it has been suggested that probably I took too much upon myself in speaking for the province of British Columbia. At the same time, I think I have the right to speak on behalf of that province more than any other member from that section of the country because I represent the finest part of the province.
Our attitude is not that of people who are opposed to any particular company. So far as I know, those of us who opposed the passage of this measure last year adopt the same attitude this year. I think I am speaking for the people of the province when I say we are prepared to withdraw our opposition, and certainly I am, the minute that the company, as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said last year, insert some five words in the charter of incorporation, that it will be an all-Canadian route. We who are opposing the bill believe that we have a great future in Canada, and particularly in western Canada. In order to fulfil that future we believe we must develop the natural resources of our country.
At this point I should like to say to my friends of the maritimes, who in many cases have not had all they should have secured from the rest of Canada, that we in the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta have done our share to see that subsidies were paid to them. We have endeavoured to see that justice was done to the maritimes. I should also like to point out to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario that they have gained their great place in the nation through the efforts and the wealth of western Canada. We hear much of the St. Lawrence waterway scheme. I should like to say to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec that the only way you can secure the fulfilment of
Alberta Natural Gas Company the St. Lawrence waterway scheme is through the support of the people of the west, and Alberta and British Columbia in particular.
And the co-operation of the United States.

I am quite prepared to talk on Canada but Harry Truman will have to look after himself. We are prepared to do our share as we have in the past. I wonder who paid for the Welland canal? We paid our share. Why? Because it developed Canada as a whole, not just Ontario. We in Alberta and British Columbia paid our share of the cost, and we are again prepared to pay our share of the cost of the development of the St. Lawrence waterway.
I want to appeal to my friends from Ontario and Quebec. When we are prepared, as we have been in the past, to do our share to develop central Canada, is it not fair that you in turn should do your part to assist us to develop the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia? To hon. members from the maritimes may I repeat that we are aware of the injustices that were done to you since confederation. I defy any member from the maritimes to say that at any time any member from the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia has done anything but support your just claims for subsidies. I am appealing particularly to the new province of Newfoundland, the tenth province, which by its entry into confederation has completed our dominion. You should realize more than any other province what it means to secure justice within your own sphere. That is all we are asking for, Mr. Speaker. We are not interested in any particular company. We are not asking for any particular subsidy or assistance, but we are asking that the resources of Canada be developed within the country for the benefit of Canadians as a whole.
Naturally I am interested in my own riding just as every other hon. member is in his. I want to digress for a minute. There are 262 members in the House of Commons, all of whom are fine men, and all of whom are sincere in endeavouring to do their duty to the best of their ability on behalf of their particular ridings and the country as a whole. There may be one exception so we will make it 261. I want them to look at things as I look at them, and not with any intention of talking against time, because I have no such intention. I want them to look at the welfare of Canada as a whole, and I particularly want them to remember that the prosperity of western Canada means their own prosperity. Too often we have had sectionalism; too often we have had one

Alberta Natural Gas Company district pulling against another, one province against another. That is not in the best interests of Canada. I maintain that this bill is designed to disrupt the economy of Canada as no other bill ever brought before us was designed to do.
For a few years, as you know, Alberta was not in the best of circumstances financially. Fortunately for them this liquid gold has come flowing from the earth and we are very glad it has, because it put Alberta in a better position than it has ever been in. It is now able to pay its way, and my information is that very shortly the provincial debt will be liquidated. Paying taxes in British Columbia, as I do, I am not so sure when we will be able to liquidate our debt; but if the action is taken that I and those who are with me recommend, I believe we will soon be in the position that Alberta is in now.
At the present time the best prospects for liquid gold on the North American continent are within the boundaries of Alberta. I am also informed that prospects are equally bright in Saskatchewan. When I say that, I am speaking only of oil and gas, and I am referring to the kind of gas we burn and use, not the kind we hear of in that province at the present time. We in the Fraser valley are of one mind on this matter. I hope during the next four years I may have the same united support, coming from all parties, as I have had on this issue. As I said before, there are not eighteen people in British Columbia who believe in this United States route. They could not even get a sponsor for this bill within our province, because not a person there believes in the southern route.
When I make that statement it is supported by the attorney general of my province. After all, you know, a federal member may be accused of speaking purely in the interests of his own riding. I have not authority to speak for the provincial government. The only person who can do that is a representative of that government. In our province we had a competition for the leadership of the party, as I believe other parties have had competitions; and the man who was defeated for the leadership became the attorney general. I do not know about other provinces, but in British Columbia the attorney general is a very important man; and I want to quote briefly what he has said. I do not want to delay things; I should like this matter to be dealt with one way or the other. I am referring now to the Calgary Herald. I do not subscribe to that newspaper, nor do I know what kind of newspaper it is. I see the name "Calgary", however, which reminds me that I went to the Grey Cup finals last


year and lost a little money on the Stampeders. Under date of February 7 this newspaper says:
B.C. declared anxious to get Alberta gas
Attorney general presents government view to hearing
Hon. Gordon Wismer, attorney general of British Columbia, said his government was anxious that natural gas be made available to the people of British Columbia "if and when the government of Alberta determines that in the interests of the people of Alberta a permit for exportation can properly be granted."
Those are the views of the attorney general of British Columbia, the province from which I come; and to the best of my ability I am trying to give the feelings of that province with respect to the export of gas.
He made the statement this morning when presenting a brief on behalf of the British Columbia government to the petroleum and natural gas conservation board of Alberta, presently hearing the application of Westcoast Transmission Company Ltd. for a licence to export gas from Alberta.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring this to the attention of hon. members from the central provinces and the maritimes, whom we have supported at all times in their demands for fair play. I ask them to pay particular attention to the remainder of this quotation.
Mr. Wismer said the British Columbia government "strongly supported the proposal that such a line should be built from northern Alberta into and through British Columbia and thence, if sufficient gas is available, to the Pacific northwest states of the United States.
I am sure hon. members will appreciate the significance of that statement, representing the views of British Columbia, urging that this line be built within Canada to serve our own people and in particular those of my province. We have reason to believe that in northern British Columbia we have oil and gas deposits equal to those of Alberta. We also believe there are deposits in northern Alberta equal to or greater than those already developed in that province. The only way these deposits can be developed is by providing an outlet. For that reason I think I am justified in reading a little further from the remarks of the attorney general of British Columbia, as they appear in the Calgary Albertan of February 8:
"If there is an exportable surplus of gas in Alberta the province of British Columbia would like to see Canadian requirements get priority over export to the United States," Hon. Gordon Wismer, attorney general for British Columbia, told the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board Tuesday.
Mr. Wismer was welcomed by the Hon. Lucien Maynard, attorney general for Alberta. Said Mr. Maynard: "We are not so callous as to be unconcerned about the misfortunes of the past few weeks in British Columbia or a possible repetition of disastrous floods. Whatever remarks or suggestions

Mr. Wismer has to make before this board, I am sure will receive the most careful consideration by the board, the people of this province, and the government."
Mr. Wismer's suggestion was this:	"We are and
have been strongly supporting the proposal that such a line (gas export) should be built from northern Alberta into and through British Columbia, and thence, if sufficient gas is available, to the Pacific northwest states of the United States of America.
That is just part of it. There has been some suggestion that we were opposed to the export of gas to the United States. Those of us who are opposing this bill are definitely of the opposite opinion. We believe that the surplus must be exported to the United States in order to make the building of the line possible. The only stand that we take is that the export of gas must be made from the Vancouver end of the line, instead of having the end of the line come into Vancouver from the United States.
I have here a copy of an advertisement that appeared in the Calgary press last year. I shall not read it in detail because one of the members from Calgary read it. This advertisement was placed in the paper by the company now applying for a charter. The city of Vancouver and the lower mainland of the Fraser valley contain about 58 per cent of the population of the province of British Columbia. One company is proposing to build an all-Canadian route, although it is definitely opposed by the company now applying for a charter. The all-Canadian route has been termed feasible by the largest firm of engineers in that line of work in the United States. This company is prepared to put that line through and deliver gas in 1952 to the city of Vancouver. This route would serve the cities of Vernon, Kamloops, Penticton, Kelowna, and have a side line to the city of Trail. We hear a good deal about this city of Trail, and I am not surprised at that. As we heard over the C.B.C. on Sunday night, Trail is one of the best developed cities in the Dominion of Canada.
While I did not see this event, owing to the fact that I was sick in bed, it was a sad sight to hear of the people of my riding lining up for two sacks of coal to which they were entitled. Alberta Natural Gas Company deliver it through the United States, and thence back into Canada. The lust for gold equals the lust for power. I have never been able to understand why some people who are multimillionaires have a greater lust for gold. Beoause this bill will not be distributed in my riding, or throughout the province generally, I am going to read the names of the directors as they appear in the bill.

maintopic: TRADE CONDITIONS-PROPOSED COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE-AMENDMENT, MR. DIEFENBAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying earlier, the trade situation in Canada today is growing desperate and fully warrants the motion that we are discussing tonight, calling for a commonwealth trade conference. In fact, information which has come to hand in a release today from the dominion bureau of statistics more than supports that statement. I shall refer to the release later and to the figures of our declining trade given in that document.
Let us look at some concrete examples of what this loss of sterling markets means to the Canadian producers. To do that we should look at the situation of our apple growers of British Columbia particularly, for theirs is a position which exemplifies perfectly the desperate need of restoring trade with the sterling markets, and the figures which I shall give, Mr. Speaker, fully justify the use of the words "the desperate need". Our apple growers are faced with the complete loss of their market in1 the United Kingdom and in this connection I intend to refer to our export figures over a series of years. However, before doing that I would like to refer to a statement made last night by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who is reported on page 288 of Hansard as follows:
The only surplus today is the surplus of cheese and1 we are carrying that right now.
Our apple growers find that the only way they can get rid of their surplus apples is to make a gift of one million boxes to the United Kingdom. The British Columbia apple growers did just that over a month ago. I find that statement of the Minister of Agriculture one of the most extraordinary made recently. It is completely unsupported by the facts. According to the government's own figures they are now carrying in storage some 28 million pounds of butter. We have a surplus position in apples in British Columbia and1 according to all appearances the 1949 crop is going to be largely unmarketed.
Our poultry producers will be amazed at the statement by the minister that there is no surplus except in cheese. Our egg producers would be glad to know where they can market their eggs. I am sure the berry growers of the Fraser valley, on whose behalf the member for that constituency raised his voice last year, will be glad to know that

there is no surplus in Canada except that of cheese and that the Minister of Agriculture is going to take care of that.
I do know that there is a surplus of apples. When we look at our export figures, when we look at what happened to our production, we see that there is a surplus. We no longer have the great export market that we used to have in the United Kingdom. Figures taken from the Canada Year Book show that from 1933 down to 1939 we exported an average of close to two million barrels of apples a year to the United Kingdom, and I ask you to bear in mind that a barrel contains a little more than three boxes. In 1936 we exported 2,202,000 barrels; in 1938, 2,473,000 barrels. In 1939, which was interrupted by the outbreak of war, we exported 1,427,000 barrels. Trade was interrupted during the war years but in 1946, the first full year of trade after the war, we exported 1,151,054 barrels to the United Kingdom or approximately 3,500,000 boxes.
In 1948 the United Kingdom purchased no apples f*om Canada, and in 1949 they purchased none. The figures show that our exports of apples pre-war and post-war up to the time when we lost the British market were approximately equal. In spite of what has been said in this house and outside the house, the figures given by the United Kingdom food officials as to their domestic requirements of apples indicate clearly that the British market is still the potential market for Canadian apples provided they can find the means to purchase them. The figures for British imports up until 1946 and 1947 as given by the United Kingdom food mission show that after the war years their imports of apples from Canada were approximately equal to the imports pre-war and that if it were not for exchange difficulties a great market for Canadian apples would still exist in the United Kingdom.
Remember that in 1948 and 1949 the United Kingdom purchased virtually no apples from Canada. The only shipments so far this year have been the million boxes sent as a gift by British Columbia. Naturally enough our apple producers are in a desperate plight. Their economy has been geared to the existence of the British market. Apple production is based on a twelve-year program. It takes from seven to eight years for a tree to begin bearing and it is at least twelve years before it reaches full production. You cannot change such a program overnight.
Certain solutions have been suggested for the difficulties in which the apple growers find themselves. An immediate solution, for this year at any rate, and for the years until there is a restoration of our markets, is the
Trade
provision of a floor or support price for the apple production of British Columbia and I believe of Nova Scotia as well. A floor price is necessary in the present emergency, but that is not the aspect I want to discuss now. I hope to have something to say about that when the agricultural estimates are up. Representations are being made to the minister and I understand that negotiations are under way so perhaps it is not timely to say anything more at the moment about a floor price.
The provision of a floor price is only a short-term solution, and a long-term solution is necessary for our agricultural problems. It seems to me that our efforts must be directed toward finding an answer to the recurring surpluses of agricultural products here in Canada. It seems to me that that could be done in one of two ways. We produce more than we can eat at home and therefore we must either sell overseas or build up our population in Canada so that it is able to consume at least a greater proportion of what we produce.
It seems to me that the aim and object of the resolution now before the house is the restoration of our overseas market. The first requirement is to remove currency restrictions. In spite of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has said, I do not think we have had any proof as yet that the imposition of currency restrictions with their resultant non-convertibility offers much hope for a solution of our trade problem. A commonwealth trade conference should be called. The imposition of restrictions hampers trade, and in this connection I should like to quote an article in the February 13 issue of Newsweek by Henry Hazlitt, the business commentator. He tells a little story which I think is apt to the matter under discussion, and I quote:
A poor peasant, according to an old folk tale, went to the wise man of his village for help and advice. The peasant lived in a one-room mud hut with his wife and four children. He was driven to desperation by the noise, the quarreling, the smell, the dirt, the poor scanty food, the poverty, sickness, and squalor in which his family lived.
"I will help you," said the wise man. So the next day he brought a male goat to the peasant's hut, saying: "You must feed this goat and take him in and let him sleep in the hut."
"Why, O wise man?" asked the peasant. "You will see," replied the wise man. "Come back to me at the turn of the moon."
On the night of the new moon the peasant was back. "O wise man, my life is unendurable. The noise in the hut is hideous. The smell is beyond belief. The goat knocks down the children and eats us out of hut and home. I am sunk in wretchedness and despair."
"I will help you," said the wise man. And he came and took away the goat. A week later the peasant came to him again, his face wreathed in smiles.

Trade
"O wise man," he said, "my life now is wonderful. You cannot imagine the change since you took away the goat! The hut is quieter. The horrible smell is gone. My family has once more almost enough to eat. How can I ever thank you enough for taking away that goat? How infinitely wise you must be to have thought of such a marvelous plan!"
We find ourselves in practically the same situation. We heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) today, in his discussion with the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) or it may have been the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), say: We are taking off these restrictions and it is having a very beneficial effect on our trade with the sterling area and the United States. Mr. Hazlitt went on to say:
I keep thinking of this tale as I read about the new plans of the bureaucrats all over the world. They impose an endless network of restrictions, burdens, coercions, and1 prohibitions on their own peoples: they all but strangle production and trade. And then their most happy solutions consist in removing one or two of the burdens and1 prohibitions that they themselves have decreed.
That is about all we have offered to us by the government in the way of prospects for increasing trade in the future. The Minister of Finance has imposed a few goats on us, and he has taken one or two away. Now he says: Look what I have done for Canadian trade. Furthermore, he says that we have had a number of conferences. There was the one in the Far East that was mentioned this afternoon which was not about trade at all. The Minister of Finance goes to Washington and discusses currency restrictions but he does not have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) with him. On another occasion the Minister of Agriculture sits down in Ottawa and discusses food contracts with the United Kingdom authorities but he does not have the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce with him. The Minister of Trade and Commerce goes overseas and discusses trade but he does not have the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Finance with him. Nevertheless the Minister of Finance said this afternoon that he thought we had had enough conferences. We have not had a single trade conference, Mr. Speaker, of the sort we are talking about, and the sort which is necessary to solve commonwealth trade relations, since the conference of 1932.
In the face of the conditions which we have described, the situation facing agriculture, the situation facing our apple growers, the situation facing the workmen of this country, it is a sort of fantastic nightmare of unreality to hear the Minister of Finance say today, when we have not had
IMr. Fulton.]
a conference yet, that another conference would serve no useful purpose and that it is not up to Canada to take the initiative.
The other solution which I mentioned is, I think, a long-term one for our agricultural problems and must go hand in hand with the efforts to build up our overseas markets again, something that can only be done by removing currency restrictions and removing them now. It is to take positive steps to build up our population at home because we produce more than we can consume. Although it will help greatly to restore overseas markets, nevertheless if that is the limit of our solution we will still be peculiarly vulnerable to any depression or upset in these overseas markets. As soon as they stop buying we will have recurring food surpluses. The two efforts must go hand in hand. Until the country begins to realize the potentialities of which it is capable, both in terms of population engaged in useful production and as a consumers' market at home to eat more of what we produce, we will be faced with the problem of recurring surpluses. Under these circumstances it is no answer to say that our effort must be in the direction of cultivating our trade with the United States. Look again at the situation of our apple producers. What prospects have Canadian apple growers in the United States market?

speechtext: Quite good.

maintopic: TRADE CONDITIONS-PROPOSED COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE-AMENDMENT, MR. DIEFENBAKER
speechtext:
Before this debate is over, perhaps the hon. member will make his contribution and tell us of the growing sales of our apples in the United States market. I will be glad to hear him substantiate his remark if my understanding of what he says is correct, namely, that the United States market offers a useful alternative to the British market. The Minister of Finance also said he would not like to have a conference without knowing what was going to be the agenda. It seems to me that a mere examination of the problem suggests the items for discussion. In order that we may have the problem fully before us, perhaps I might now refer to the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin which was released today, February 28. The first paragraph reads:
Canada's domestic exports to the United States- for the third successive month-were substantially higher in value in January than a year earlier. Shipments to commonwealth and other countries were generally lower and the total value of domestic exports to all countries fell below that of January last year.
Further down it continues:
Total exports to all countries in January declined in value to $221,200,000 compared with $237 million a year earlier.

I might interpolate that this was a reduction of $16 million. The release continues:
Shipments to the United States thus accounted for about 59 per cent of the month's total value as compared with slightly more than 50 per cent in the twelve months of 1949.
But the position is that our over-all trade picture is deteriorating. The release goes on as follows:
Sales to the United Kingdom-which have been subject to fluctuations during recent months-were valued at $48,608,000, down from $55,813,000 a year earlier, but only slightly under the December figure.
We might point out that in January sales to the United Kingdom declined by over $7 million. Continuing it reads:
There were decreases also from a year ago in exports to other commonwealth areas. The largest decline was in exports to commonwealth countries in Asia which fell to $3,473,000 from $14,937,000, with shipments to India down to $495,000 from $11,190,000 in January last year. . . . Exports to the British West Indies, including British Guiana, Bermuda and British Honduras, declined to $2,512,000 compared to $4,608,000; to commonwealth countries in Africa to $3,831,000 from $4,991,000; and to the Oceania group of Australia, New Zealand and Fiji to $2,612,000 from $3,145,000.
The paragraph concludes with this sentence:
Total value of exports to all commonwealth countries, including the United Kingdom, was $62,336,000 as against $83,706,000.
For the month of January, Mr. Speaker, there was a decline in our exports to commonwealth countries of $21 million.
With that general background, together with the knowledge all hon. members have of the situation facing individual producers or producer groups in their own constituencies, it is no answer for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to say that a conference would not serve any useful purpose, and that he does not know just what such a conference might discuss. A conference might discuss ways and means of restoring trade, of removing trade restrictions, of trading between commonwealth countries to our mutual benefit. It might discuss the removal of currency restrictions; it might discuss the kind of goods available in one country for shipment to another and the kind of goods that can be shipped back, and a means of providing for the balance of payments resulting. It might also discuss immigration and emigration as between commonwealth countries. There are many things such a conference might discuss, problems the Canadian people want to see solved. They are problems for which the government so far has offered no solution. While it is not generous to decry the efforts that have been made by various ministers and missions who have been sent abroad, I think it is
Trade
fair to say that these isolated, separate missions hither and yon all over the map, each consisting of an individual minister or group of experts without any co-ordination such as a trade conference must have, are foredoomed to failure in attempting to deal with the trade situation faced today by this country and the world in general.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to echo what has been said before by hon. members on this side of the house and what I know is in the hearts of all members on all sides. Canada's greatest customer over the years, the nation or group of nations that has taken more from us than it has sold to us, is the British commonwealth of nations and particularly the United Kingdom. We would be making a grave mistake if, as one hon. member put it, we sold that commonwealth short. The fact is that owing to currency restrictions the United Kingdom can no longer buy from us more than she sells to us, because the currency she has with which to pay for what she buys is not convertible. That is the problem that must be solved if we want to restore commonwealth trade and if we want to halt the trend which is going on, as the release issued today by the dominion bureau of statistics makes quite clear.
Together with other hon. members who have spoken this afternoon, in behalf of the group of producers I mentioned specifically, the apple producers of British Columbia, but also in behalf of the lumber producers of that province and of the maritimes and of all Canadian producers of goods which other people need, I hope the government will not close its mind to the necessity of a conference such as that suggested in the amendment moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the beneficial results which could flow from it.

maintopic: TRADE CONDITIONS-PROPOSED COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE-AMENDMENT, MR. DIEFENBAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to speak briefly to the amendment now before the house, which asks that the government take immediate steps to convene, at the earliest possible date, a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets and thereby provide jobs for the Canadian people.
Without agreeing with the Progressive Conservative opposition that our trade situation is in a desperate way, and without agreeing with the government that the position is a matter of no great concern, I think there is a general feeling that not only Canadian but world trade relations are getting into

Trade
difficulties. In my view this would not necessarily be a serious matter were it not for the fact that, as I see it, the present deterioration in trade and in world economic conditions follows a pattern we know so well. That was the pattern after the last war, when we had a few short years of economic activity when we were urged by businessmen to produce more and consume less. But shortly came the debacle, when a great many people could not consume at all, not because the things were not there to consume but because something had gone wrong with the exchange of commodities both between nations and within the nation. At the present time we see the very same pattern developing. When we finished the war we had a tremendous backlog of needs to be met, both in consumer and capital goods. This was more so with the countries of Europe than on this continent of North America, but in four or five short years we have overcome that backlog of consumer needs, we have added to our capital resources so that now we can supply a greater amount of goods and services than ever before. Now, the paradox of the situation is this: just when we are better equipped than ever before to supply the needs of our people and raise the standard of living, the standard of living is going down. How far that deterioration may go on this particular lap I do not know; but if we do not find some way to distribute the wealth we can produce so abundantly, nothing can save us from falling into a depression such as we had from 1930 to 1939, from which we were rescued by the war.
Whether, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has said, the present trade slump is not due to a lack of conferences, or whether it would not necessarily be improved by calling another conference, certainly I believe one thing is true; that is, that it will not settle itself. Either we are going to try to find a solution for our problems in such ways as solutions can be found, or we are going to throw up our hands and say there is nothing further we can do. For that reason alone, I would favour a trade conference. I am sure that once representatives met at such a conference they would not only discuss the matter of the exchange of commodities, but they could discuss the underlying difficulties, economic conditions and methods of distributing wealth, as well as the mere exchange of commodities.
During the last two sessions, I have been appalled to hear members stand up in this house and condemn the British government for its refusal to buy more Canadian goods. I believe that anyone who has sufficient intelligence to become a member of this house,

and who makes a statement of that kind, is unpardonably ignorant. If the Minister of Agriculture made the statement that was attributed to him to the effect that there was some conspiracy in the United Kingdom not to buy Canadian goods, then I have not words to express what I think of that.
It is the generally accepted understanding of international trade that the goods we import are paid1 for by the goods we export. If we have no goods to export, then we will have to stop importing goods; that is the general picture. Let us look at the situation as between Canada and the United Kingdom. I have in my hand a copy of Foreign Trade, a publication issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This issue is dated February 8, 1950. I find that the total Canadian exports to the United Kingdom for the calendar year 1949, excluding gold, amounted to $705 million; that was the value of the goods we exported to the United Kingdom. We bought from the United Kingdom goods to the value of $307,400,000. In other words, for every dollar's worth of goods we bought from the United Kingdom, the United Kingdom bought $2.30 worth of goods from us. Unless there is some way by which the United Kingdom can get dollars or gold, she cannot buy anything more from us than she is buying. It is sheer nonsense, it is sheer hypocrisy, for members of this house to complain about the United Kingdom not buying more goods from Canada.
Let us look at the picture as between Canada and the United States. For the same calendar year of 1949, we sold to the United States goods totalling $1,503 million. We bought from the United States goods totalling $1,954 million. In other words, for every dollar's worth of goods we sold to the United States, we bought $1.30 worth of goods from the United States. Bear in mind that it gives us great concern to conserve our dollars, so that we can continue to buy from the United States. Supposing the trade picture between the United1 States and Canada were represented by Canada buying $2.30* worth of goods from the United States for every dollar's worth of goods the United States bought from us, would the Minister of Finance be so emphatic about the value of non-discrimination in trade as he was this afternoon?
In 1947 when we imposed restrictions on United States imports there was a certain amount of tongue in the cheek attitude on the question of non-discrimination. Although the balance of payments was not nearly as bad as it is today between Canada and the United Kingdom, restrictions on imports from! the United States were imposed, the same restrictions being imposed on imports from other

countries, including the United Kingdom. But I heard the Minister of Finance say in this house that although it was quite true we were imposing the same restrictions on the United Kingdom, it did not matter because we were not buying any of the prohibited goods from the United Kingdom. It seems to me we should be realistic in these matters and realize that we cannot sell to a country very much more than we buy from that country. All the nations of the world must realize, and for the purpose of what I am saying now I mean the nations of the free world, that if they are going to expand1 their economies, increase prosperity, raise the standard of living of their people, then we will have to do much more and go much further than we have so far in the matter of deciding what we can sell to each other, and what we can buy from each other.
In my opinion, it is not just a question of improving Canada's trade position, it is a question of international prosperity-the prosperity of the countries of the western world. But it is more than that; it is as much a part of our defence against aggression as is our military preparedness. If we do not keep the western world prosperous, we will lose out in the struggle with the totalitarian world. Let us remember that to maintain the prosperity of the western world is part of our defence against aggression. It is for that reason this question is so important- That is why increasing unemployment and falling markets are so important to everyone who believes in co-operation and peace. We also must not forget that we cannot have co-operation in military matters to defend ourselves against an enemy, and have trade wars between the co-operators. Surely the time has arrived when we should see that that sort of economics no longer fits the needs of the world of 1950. Whether or not a conference of this kind would accomplish anything, surely it would be an advance if we could bring the nations of the commonwealth close together-the commonwealth now is both east and west-and find out more definitely what each nation has to sell and what each is willing to buy. Surely if we did not do anything more than make an advance in that direction, the conference would be worth while. Unless those who are opposed to such a conference have some better solution for meeting our economic problems, they certainly should not turn this one down without giving a serious consideration indeed.

Before putting the question,
I should like to observe that I have had some doubt as to whether the amendment is in order under our rules.
It is true that wide latitude is given in respect of amendments to the motion for going into supply. It is equally true, however, that there are well-established classes of amendments which, for good reason, cannot be moved on such a motion. For instance, a matter of which notice has been given or which stands upon the order paper cannot be introduced as an amendment to a motion for going into supply. See Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, at page 420.
The opening clause of the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), reads as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers have:
(1) failed to take adequate measures to preserve and expand markets for Canada's surplus products of farm, forest, sea and mine, and to deal with the problems of increasing unemployment and reduced income to Canadian farmers and other producers;...
The present amendment is similar to the amendment just quoted in that it deals with a particular phase or aspect of the broader question, and recommends a particular method for resolving it. The subject matter of the present amendment could be, and I believe already has been, introduced in the debate on the address.
I feel bound to disclose to the house the doubt I entertain as to the admissibility of this amendment. It is a borderline case, but I think that the doubt should be resolved in favour of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). For that reason I am not going to rule the amendment out of order.

Mr. Speaker, in my opening remarks last evening I had intended to make reference to the illustrious group of governmental supporters in this corner of the house. pull our own weight and in time it is our hope that we will be able to lend a lot to other sections of the house.
Continuing along the theme of trade with Great Britain and the so-called lost returns to our farmers, I have a few observations I should like to add to what I had to say last evening. Our good friends in the official opposition have suggested various sums that have been lost because of the contracts that were made for prices below the world level. We are not in disagreement with the statement that the prices were below world level, but why in heaven's name are they not consistent in their arguments?
One hon. member will get up and make a tear-jerking speech with reference to the commonwealth and the British people, and then in the next minute another speaker gets up and says that this country has lost $500 million. Then a day or two later another speaker gets up and says that we lost $1,000 million. Then another fellow, not to be outdone, says that we have lost $2,000 million.

You answer for your own head or for your own seat and I will answer for mine. If anyone stops to consider the limited number of dollars that Great Britain had during the post-war years and where those dollars came from he will not suggest that we should have kept prices up to the world level. The government with which I happen to have the honour to be associated and will be associated with is the government that inaugurated this program. They supplied the dollars with which Great Britain bought our products.
The Canadian taxpayer makes a great holler about the atrocious taxes, but I can assure you that if prices had been fixed at the world level it would have meant so many more dollars that the taxpayer would have had to supply to Great Britain. Do not forget that Great Britain had only a limited number of dollars to spend and as a consequence this government made a deal to provide them with opportunities to purchase the foodstuffs that they could use.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was not in his seat last night when I made this remark, so I am going to make it again. He has confused the 16 per cent decline in farm revenues with that of trade. He states there has been a 16 per cent decline in income.

Call it field crops or anything you like, it does not make any difference. We will call it field crops. Before trade can be carried on, goods must be produced and hence the 16 per cent decline is not the result of trade but is an internal production decline due to drought conditions. As a matter of fact when you consider the amount of money that we produce in the west from the sale of our products from year to year, and the fact that about one-third of the province of Saskatchewan has no crop, a 16 per cent decline is only a fraction of the over-all total production.
Much has been said, is being said and no doubt will continue to be said about what Great Britain has done for the commonwealth. I quite agree. As the expression goes, Great Britain cast her bread on the waters and it came back as ham sandwiches. Nevertheless I do not want anyone to forget that everything that Great Britain has been and is today is directly attributable to what she got from the commonwealth. In other words, if she continues on her present path of reneging on what we in Canada feel she should do, it is not beyond the realms of possibility she may some day be sitting alone, a lonely little island on the threshold of Europe. The businessmen of Great Britain are noted for their shrewdness. They are just the same as every individual in this House of Commons. The opposition party or parties would be the first people in the Dominion of Canada to criticize the government if they were to buy from any country a product which they could secure cheaper elsewhere. The same thing applies to the British empire. They are going to buy where they can do so most cheaply.
