Mr. Speaker, this is the second time it has been my privilege to rise in this house and take part in a debate on the speech from the throne. In my first remarks I should like to congratulate the mover and seconder, who performed their tasks so well. I shall try to be as brief as possible, but I believe it is my duty to bring to this house matters which I feel have to do with the welfare and future of the coming generation.
As a railroad man I also feel that it is my duty to say a few words with respect to a matter which has been mentioned several times in the house during the last few days; that is, the shortage of coal which has caused a decrease in passenger service on the Canadian National Railways. After thirty-seven years of railroad work I believe I know the routine of its administration; and I feel that we should not be so ready to criticize our railways, which have made such a contribution to the development of this country. It is true that a lack of coal has forced a curtailment of passenger service by the Canadian National; but let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the financial position of our railway companies is not what it should be, and they are obliged to carry on at a loss while giving our people the best service possible. I am sure a great deal of the criticism that is being expressed comes from members of this house who never travel by train if they can possibly get where they are going by car or by plane. Our railway officials have believed it better to maintain the freight service so the people of the country would suffer as little as possible, and have chosen to reduce passenger service instead; and I congratulate them on having done so. It is necessary that those in charge of our railways should look to the future of this country, and at the same time increase the efficiency of our railways and develop more speedy transportation in order to compete with other methods of transportation. So I say we should not reproach those who are making every effort to develop rail transportation in this country. Affiliated with those companies we have ocean transportation and large hotels which give accommodation to the people of Canada and also provide essential facilities for our tourists.
342	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gosselin
I repeat that the railway companies have greatly assisted in the development of this country. When there was no other form of either passenger or freight service, the railway companies carried on, even at a loss; and as a railroad man for so many years I greatly regret to hear this criticism. Instead of hon. members criticizing they should bear in mind that it is the duty of those administering the affairs of these companies to protect their finances and, in so doing, protect the finances of the country.
Then I should like to congratulate the government on doing everything possible to increase the value of education in this country; yet I am afraid I must say that to a certain extent education has been neglected. An educated population is the most important asset any country may have. I believe that, in many ways, education has been neglected, and that our governments should have taken a more active part in giving the necessary financial assistance to the raising of our educational standards. During the last few years our provincial governments, which are charged with the responsibility for education, no doubt owing to a shortage of finances, were forced to neglect the education of our children. The federal government recognized its duty to enter this field and assist the provinces in providing better education. This will mean, Mr. Speaker, that the professor and' the teacher will receive a better income than they have in the past. The character of our children, which is formed in the schoolroom, is carried through life. There is, therefore, no more important question than the provision of an education for the future population of our country.
I wish once more, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the government on its efforts to assist our provincial governments in carrying forward the principle of education to such an extent that no public man who has that right may criticize the educational standards we have set. I wish to congratulate the government also on the action it has taken in connection with health. There is no category of social service which is more essential, Mr. Speaker, than health services. This is especially true in the years we are going through, because our population is in the mids of dangerous and contagious diseases. I feel it is the duty of the government, regardless of any other department, to use the money necessary to establish hospitalization and medical care for our population. This would enable our people to look forward to all the medical care that is necessary throughout their life.
Regrettably, Mr. Speaker, in this young country of ours, it is impossible to carry on everything at once. I still believe that this


government is establishing a sound foundation for social services. I believe that program can be divided into two principal parts, health and education. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that an educated and healthy population is the fundamental basis for the prosperity of any country. I urge the government not to withdraw on those fundamental principles, which are of importance to the welfare of this Canada of ours.
There is another important question, Mr. Speaker, and that is ensuring the aged a pension sufficient to take care of their needs. After spending the greater part of his life-in the raising of a family, the aged person will feel that he is protected. I hope that this government will look into this matter, and find a way of guaranteeing the older element of our population a satisfactory pension without a means test. The old age-pension, as it is now, is highly appreciated, but I do believe it does not go far enough. I do not like the old age pension being recognized as a matter of charity. Those who have attained the age of 65 or 70, who have given their entire life to their country, are often, obliged to degrade themselves to seek this form of charity. I am sure that this government will investigate every possible means' of giving these people an old age pension without a means test, so that those who deserve it will not feel there is the stigma of charity attached to it. I know that to-many of us, Mr. Speaker, such a pension system seems to be beyond our financial capability. I am sure, however, that the administration of this country will provide someway of overcoming the financial situation, and will solve this problem.
May I congratulate this government on the-adoption of family allowances. This administration found the means with which to pay those family allowances to all families, regardless of wealth. This ensures that the younger element of our population will be provided' with the necessities of life.
My next remarks, Mr. Speaker, will be designed to give assistance to this government in regard to agriculture. As I stated a few moments ago, I am a railroad man by profession, but I am also a farmer. I am one of those who have followed the occupation of farming since childhood. I am the son of a farmer, and I intend to bend all my efforts towards improving the welfare and ensuring the prosperity of farmers. The farmers in my day, Mr. Speaker, as everyone will admit, were far from prosperous. They were not encouraged to remain on the soil. In the last few years new developments have taken place, as a result of which our products are sold to better advantage. Our agricultural

schools have also developed ways and means of obtaining higher revenues for those engaged in farming. But I believe that the present government, or any other government, should give consideration to further measures to ensure the prosperity of our farmers, who are fundamentally the basis of the prosperity and the guarantee of the financial stability of any country in the world. That being so, no government should neglect to maintain their stability, for by so doing they will be guaranteeing the financial stability of the country whose affairs they are called upon to administer.
Before going further in my remarks with regard to the farming situation, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who is a farmer himself and understands the necessity of maintaining the farmers on the soil. He knows that it is more than ever necessary to provide them with a comfortable living on their farms. He knows that is his duty, and he has shown that he recognizes it by providing for the farmers subsidies commensurate with the financial situation of the country.
We have often heard it said, in the last few months especially, that the farmer is neglected and is going to be discouraged. I say no. As I have said on several occasions, especially in this house before a group of administrators of the country, we should gather together to maintain those principles of guaranteeing prosperity to the farmers, who are, as we all understand, the basis of financial stability, instead of making speeches that may cause them to become discouraged, and stating that within six months or a year our farmers will be in a disastrous position because there is no market for their products. Let us have more confidence in the future, Mr. Speaker. Let us have more confidence that any public man who is willing to devote himself to public life, no matter to what party he may belong, will give this encouragement. Regardless of what the political beliefs of my farmer colleagues in this house may be, I should have preferred to hear them tell the government that at the present time we are facing a decrease in the value of our products but have confidence that we may trade with foreign countries and with the United States so that they may absorb the surplus and that we may maintain our prices for our farm products. By doing so, instead of trying to discourage them in a small political way, I believe they would have rendered a service to the farming community. I state this with all the sincerity that I as a farmer possess, as a result of my experience over many years.
The Address-Mr. Gosselin
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that after a war it is necessary for an adjustment to be made in the financial situation of a country. No doubt the United Kingdom faces the same problem that we face here, namely a readjustment of finances; and they find themselves in a position in which they are unable to make purchases in sterling and to expand further the exchange of commodities, as has been explained in this house. I believe that it is necessary for all countries to look at the past, but I also believe that it is necessary for them to look to the future. With all the sincerity of which we are capable we hope that we shall not be called on again to face the rigours of another war. If our debts were raised to such an extent, our working population would require higher salaries in order to maintain their families, and this would of necessity cause an increase in the payrolls of their employers. But let us hope once more that we shall not be forced to face another war.
May I congratulate the government on the principles they are adopting to try to readjust all categories of finance in order to protect this country of ours and its future. It is necessary for this house to group together, regardless of politics, and study ways and means of giving to our younger element the encouragement they deserve so that they will not feel themselves in the desert after having had the advantages of-and I feel I must say this-extravagant living as compared with that which men of my age and many years younger have experienced in the past. I do not say this by way of reproach, and I hope that I am not misunderstood. Because of the high revenues in all categories of employment, and the return we receive, we as fathers of families were not obliged to provide a real education in economy as was done in the past. May I therefore once more congratulate the present government on providing, by every possible means, that the finances of this country shall be on a sound basis so that the bondholders of this country shall never have reason to fear that their savings are in danger. It is the duty of the government to look first to the guarantee of its obligations; second, to adopt social laws so that its population may have faith in their security; and third, to establish trade with other countries, and the exchange of commodities in order to ensure the sale of our surplus products. I know that the present government are working on that principle, that they are looking forward, and that they are more advanced than the opposition seems to give them credit for in this house.
344	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gosselin
I have confidence that when it becomes necessary to export goods to the United Kingdom arrangements will be made, and we shall be assured that we shall continue to trade with the United Kingdom and also with our good neighbour, the United States. We should express words of encouragement to those with whom we are in communication; we should not try to instil il their minds the thought that we are gone forever. It is most important to our country to create in our minds the feeling that the future is worth boking forward to. We should not try to discourage the younger element by saying that the future before them is dark. No matter how we feel, we hold a responsible position in this house, and we should try to eliminate all expressions which might lead any of our younger element to believe that the future before them is dark. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe that every public man will do his duty toward the welfare and the future of the couritry in which he lives.
I believe that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will provide ways and means of assisting our farmers to increase production.

speechtext:
Hon. members on the opposite side speak of surplus production. We should not look forward to the future as something black; we should do our work and conduct our activities as though the future were bright, and in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred I believe that success will crown our efforts.
I hope .that the Minister of Agriculture, in his present capacity, will, in co-operation with the provincial authorities, give the necessary assistance to our farmers to increase production, and that that increased production will be brought about with the same amount of work. By so doing we will give our farmers encouragement to harvest their crops and to deliver the surplus which they will be able to offer to the labourer, at a reduction in price. In that way the farmer will be able to deliver the commodities of his farm to the cities at a lower rate, a rate which will compare with the reduction which is necessary among our working classes in order to stabilize conditions in this country.

May I give an example. So far as wages are concerned, the working classes have no desire to increase wages beyond what is necessary at the end of the week to take care of the obligations which they have toward their families and to buy the necessities for the table. Because of the high prices of commodities it is necessary for the labouring man to ask for an increase in wages.
I remember that during the years from 1914 to 1918' railroad employees were given increases in wages, and after the financial situation became stabilized, the credit for which should no doubt go to the government of the day, a reduction in salary took place in 1923 to compare with the reduction in the cost of living. It was accepted with assurance and satisfaction, as the working classes could buy with that amount of money that which was unattainable before. Farming is the basis of prosperity, and agricultural products are necessities to all classes of people. The farmer should be provided with ways and means to increase production. He should have guaranteed to him the financial assistance which is necessary to enable him to carry on in such a way as to give to himself and family all that is essential to encourage them to remain on the soil. High salaries and short hours of work that prevail in the cities should not be introduced on the farms.
A few days ago one hon. member mentioned that the hours the farmer works are unlimited. I agree with his remarks. However, I believe that if the farmer is given a reasonable return for the long hours he works he and his sons will not be apt to desert the soil.
On motion of Mr. Gosselin the debate was adjourned.
